allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH and advanced age, aneurysm treatment is reasonable, after careful discussion of prognosis with family members, to improve survival and outcome.
drivingTrials: Barrow Ruptured Aneurysm Trial (BRAT) Substudy (Catapano et al. 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH who do not improve after correction of modifiable conditions and are deemed unsalvageable because of evidence of irreversible neurological injury, treatment of the aneurysm is not beneficial.
In patients with acute onset of severe headache, prompt diagnostic workup and evaluation are recommended to diagnose/exclude aSAH and minimize morbidity and mortality.

In patients with acute onset of severe headache who present >6 hours from symptom onset or who have a new neurological deficit, a noncontrast head CT and, if negative for aSAH, lumbar puncture (LP) should be performed to diagnose/exclude aSAH.

In patients with acute onset of severe headache who present <6 hours from symptom onset and without new neurological deficit, a noncontrast head CT performed on a high-quality scanner and interpreted by a board-certified neuroradiologist is reasonable to diagnose/exclude aSAH.
drivingTrials: Meta-Analysis by Dubosh et al. 2016 (8907 patients

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with acute onset of severe headache without a new neurological deficit, application of the Ottawa SAH Rule may be reasonable to identify those at high risk for aSAH.

In patients with spontaneous SAH with high level of concern for aneurysmal source and a negative or inconclusive CT angiography (CTA), digital subtraction angiography (DSA) is indicated to diagnose/exclude cerebral aneurysm(s).
In patients with SAH from confirmed cerebral aneurysm(s), DSA can be useful to determine the optimal strategy for aneurysm intervention.

For patients with aSAH, timely transfer from hospitals with low case volume to higher-volume centers with multidisciplinary neurointensive care services, comprehensive stroke center capabilities, and experienced cerebrovascular surgeons/neuroendovascular interventionalists is recommended to improve outcomes.
For patients with aSAH, care should be provided in a dedicated neurocritical care unit by a multidisciplinary team.
drivingTrials: PRINCE Study Part 1 & 2 (Venkatasubba Rao et al. 2020

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH and unsecured aneurysm, frequent blood pressure (BP) monitoring and BP control with short-acting medication(s) is recommended to avoid severe hypotension, hypertension, and BP variability.
In patients with aSAH who are receiving anticoagulants, emergency anticoagulation reversal with appropriate reversal agents should be performed to prevent rebleeding.
drivingTrials: NCS/SCCM Antithrombotic Reversal Guideline (Frontera et al. 2016)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, routine use of antifibrinolytic therapy is not useful to improve functional outcome.
drivingTrials: ULTRA Landmark RCT (Post et al. Lancet 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with aSAH, surgical or endovascular treatment of the ruptured aneurysm should be performed as early as feasible after presentation, preferably within 24 hours of onset, to improve outcome.
For patients with aSAH, complete obliteration of the ruptured aneurysm is indicated whenever feasible to reduce the risk of rebleeding and retreatment.

For patients with aSAH in whom complete obliteration of the ruptured aneurysm by either clipping or primary coiling treatment is not feasible in the acute phase, partial obliteration to secure the rupture site and retreatment in a delayed fashion in those with functional recovery are reasonable to prevent rebleeding.
For patients with aSAH from ruptured aneurysms of the posterior circulation that are amenable to coiling, coiling is indicated in preference to clipping to improve outcome.
For patients with aSAH deemed salvageable and with depressed level of consciousness due to large intraparenchymal hematoma, emergency clot evacuation should be performed to reduce mortality.
drivingTrials: Heiskanen et al. 1988 (RCT showing 27% vs 80% mortality benefit)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with aSAH, the ruptured aneurysm should be evaluated by specialist(s) with endovascular and surgical expertise to determine the relative risks and benefits of surgical or endovascular treatment according to patient and aneurysm characteristics.
For patients >70 years of age with aSAH, the superiority of coiling or clipping to improve outcome is not well established.
drivingTrials: ISAT Trial Subgroup Analysis (Molyneux et al. 2005

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients <40 years of age with aSAH, clipping of the ruptured aneurysm might be considered the preferred mode of treatment to improve durability of the treatment and outcome.
drivingTrials: ISAT Trial Subgroup Analysis (Molyneux et al. 2005

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with good-grade aSAH from ruptured aneurysms of the anterior circulation equally suitable for both primary coiling and clipping, primary coiling is recommended in preference to clipping to improve 1-year functional outcome.
drivingTrials: ISAT Landmark RCT (Molyneux et al. Lancet 2002

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with good-grade aSAH from ruptured aneurysms of the anterior circulation equally suitable for both primary coiling and clipping, both treatment options are reasonable to achieve favorable long-term outcome.
drivingTrials: ISAT Long-Term Follow-up (van Donkelaar et al. 2020

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with aSAH from ruptured wide-neck aneurysms not amenable to surgical clipping or primary coiling, endovascular treatment with stent-assisted coiling or flow diverters is reasonable to reduce the risk of rebleed.
For patients with aSAH from ruptured fusiform/blister aneurysms, the use of flow diverters is reasonable to reduce mortality.
For patients with aSAH from ruptured saccular aneurysms amenable to either primary coiling or clipping, stents or flow diverters should not be used to avoid higher risk of complications.
In patients with aSAH, the intraoperative use of mannitol or hypertonic saline can be effective in reducing ICP and cerebral edema.
In patients with aSAH, anesthetic goals should include minimizing postprocedural pain, nausea, and vomiting.
In patients with aSAH, prevention of intraoperative hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia during aneurysm surgery is reasonable to improve outcomes.
In patients with aSAH and an unsecured ruptured aneurysm, frequent intraoperative BP monitoring and BP control are reasonable to prevent ischemia and rerupture.
In patients with aSAH, intraoperative neuromonitoring may be reasonable to guide anesthetic and operative management.

In patients with aSAH and an uncontrolled intraoperative aneurysmal rupture, adenosine may be considered to facilitate aneurysm clip placement by inducing cardiac standstill and temporary profound pause.
In patients with good-grade aSAH, the routine use of induced mild hypothermia during aneurysm surgery is not beneficial.
drivingTrials: IHAST Landmark RCT (Todd et al. NEJM 2005

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH who require mechanical ventilation for >24 hours, implementation of a standardized ICU care bundle is recommended to reduce the duration of mechanical ventilation and hospital-acquired pneumonia.
drivingTrials: BI-VILI Quality Improvement Project (Asehnoune et al. Intensive Care Med 2017)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH who develop severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and life-threatening hypoxemia, rescue maneuvers such as prone positioning and alveolar recruitment maneuvers with ICP monitoring may be reasonable to improve oxygenation.
In patients with aSAH, close monitoring and goal-directed treatment of volume status are reasonable to maintain euvolemia.
In patients with aSAH, use of mineralocorticoids is reasonable to treat natriuresis and hyponatremia.
In patients with aSAH, induction of hypervolemia is potentially harmful because of the association with excess morbidity.
In patients with aSAH whose ruptured aneurysm has been secured, pharmacological or mechanical venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis is recommended to reduce the risk for VTE.
drivingTrials: CLOTS 3 Landmark RCT (Dennis et al. Lancet 2013

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, effective glycemic control, strict hyperglycemia management, and avoidance of hypoglycemia are reasonable to improve outcome.
In patients with aSAH with fever refractory to antipyretic medications, the effectiveness of therapeutic temperature management (TTM) during the acute phase of aSAH is uncertain.
drivingTrials: PAIS Trial (den Hertog et al. Lancet Neurol 2009)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, use of evidence-based protocols and order sets is recommended to improve standardization of care.
drivingTrials: QASC Cluster RCT (Middleton et al. Lancet 2011

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, frequent neurological assessment with a neurological assessment tool such as the GCS or National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is recommended to monitor DCI and other secondary complications.
drivingTrials: VASOGRADE Scale (de Oliveira Manoel et al. Stroke 2015)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, frequent vital sign and neurological monitoring is recommended for detection of neurological change and prevention of secondary cerebral insults and poor outcomes.
In patients with aSAH, a validated dysphagia screening protocol should be implemented before initiation of oral intake to reduce the incidence of pneumonia.
In patients with aSAH, specialized nursing stroke competencies and certification can be effective to positively affect outcomes, timeliness of care, and adherence to stroke protocols.
In patients with aSAH and a secured aneurysm, an early, evidence-based mobility algorithm is reasonable to improve level of function at discharge and global functional outcome at 12 months.
In patients with aSAH with suspected vasospasm or limited neurological examination, CTA or CT perfusion (CTP) can be useful to detect vasospasm and predict DCI.
In patients with aSAH, transcranial Doppler (TCD) ultrasound monitoring is reasonable to detect vasospasm and predict DCI.
In patients with high-grade aSAH, continuous EEG (cEEG) monitoring can be useful to predict DCI.
In patients with high-grade aSAH, invasive monitoring of brain tissue oxygenation, lactate/pyruvate ratio, and glutamate may be considered to predict DCI.
In patients with aSAH, early initiation of enteral nimodipine is beneficial in preventing DCI and improving functional outcomes.
drivingTrials: Allen et al. Landmark NEJM Trial 1983

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, maintaining euvolemia can be beneficial in preventing DCI and improving functional outcomes.
In patients with aSAH and symptomatic vasospasm, elevating systolic BP values may be reasonable to reduce the progression and severity of DCI.
In patients with aSAH and severe vasospasm, use of intra-arterial vasodilator therapy may be reasonable to reverse cerebral vasospasm and reduce the progression and severity of DCI.
In patients with aSAH and severe vasospasm, cerebral angioplasty may be reasonable to reverse cerebral vasospasm and reduce the progression and severity of DCI.
drivingTrials: BPAV Phase II RCT (Zwienenberg-Lee et al. 2008)

no significant benefit in DCI or mortality)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, routine use of intravenous magnesium to improve neurological outcomes is not recommended.
drivingTrials: IMASH Phase III RCT (Wong et al. Stroke 2010)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with aSAH at risk of DCI, prophylactic hemodynamic augmentation should not be performed to reduce iatrogenic patient harm.
In patients with aSAH and acute symptomatic hydrocephalus, urgent CSF diversion (EVD and/or lumbar drainage) should be performed to improve neurological outcome.

In patients with aSAH and hydrocephalus who require an EVD, implementation and adherence to an EVD bundled protocol that addresses insertion, management, education, and monitoring are recommended to reduce complication and infection rates.
In patients with aSAH and associated chronic symptomatic hydrocephalus, permanent CSF diversion is recommended to improve neurological outcome.
In patients with aSAH, routine fenestration of the lamina terminalis is not indicated for reducing the rate of shunt dependency.
drivingTrials: Meta-Analysis by Komotar et al. 2009 (11 studies

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH and either fluctuating neurological examination, depressed mental state, ruptured MCA aneurysm, high-grade SAH, ICH, hydrocephalus, or cortical infarction, cEEG monitoring is reasonable to detect seizures.

In patients with aSAH and high-seizure-risk features (ie, ruptured MCA aneurysm, high-grade SAH, ICH, hydrocephalus, and cortical infarction), use of prophylactic antiseizure medication(s) may be reasonable to prevent seizures.

In patients with aSAH without high-seizure-risk features (ie, ruptured MCA aneurysm, high-grade SAH, ICH, hydrocephalus, and cortical infarction), prophylactic treatment with antiseizure medication is not beneficial.
In patients with aSAH, phenytoin for seizure prevention and/or antiseizure prophylaxis is associated with excess morbidity and mortality.
In patients with aSAH who present with seizures, treatment with antiseizure medications for ≤7 days is reasonable to reduce seizure-related complications in the perioperative period.
In patients with aSAH without prior epilepsy who present with seizures, treatment with antiseizure medications beyond 7 days is not effective for reducing future SAH-associated seizure risk.
In patients with aSAH, use of validated grading scores or patient-reported outcome measures prior to hospital discharge is recommended to screen for physical, cognitive, behavioral, and QOL deficits.
In patients with aSAH, use of validated screening tools in the postacute period is recommended to identify post-aSAH depression and anxiety.
In patients with aSAH and depression, psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy are recommended to reduce symptoms of depression.
drivingTrials: Legg et al. Cochrane SSRI Review 2019 (RR 0.75)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, use of a validated screening tool in the postacute period is useful to identify cognitive dysfunction.
In patients with aSAH, an early multidisciplinary team–based approach to treatment and rehabilitation is recommended to reduce LOS and identify discharge needs.
drivingTrials: Alaraj et al. 2017 (LOS reduced from 21.6 to 14.1 days)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH and no other medical or neurological contraindications, early rehabilitation after the ruptured aneurysm is secured is reasonable to improve functional outcome and reduce LOS.
In patients with aSAH in a coma, early use of neurostimulants may be reasonable to promote consciousness recovery.
In patients with aSAH without depression, fluoxetine therapy is not effective to enhance poststroke functional status.
In adult patients with aSAH, screening and intervention for depression, anxiety, and sexual dysfunction are recommended to improve long-term outcomes.
drivingTrials: von Vogelsang et al. EQ-5D 10-Yr Study 2013

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH, it is reasonable to choose the MoCA over the MMSE to identify cognitive impairment.
In patients with aSAH, counseling patients and caregivers on the high long-term risk of cognitive dysfunction can be beneficial to identify long-term needs.
drivingTrials: Corraini et al. 30-Year Cohort Study 2017 (HR for dementia 2.72)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 10. Risk Factors & Monitoring for Recurrent aSAH
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH who have undergone aneurysm repair, perioperative cerebrovascular imaging is recommended to identify remnants or recurrence of the aneurysm that may require further treatment.

allPracticeChanges.topic: 10. Risk Factors & Monitoring for Recurrent aSAH
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with aSAH who have undergone aneurysm repair, follow-up cerebrovascular imaging is recommended to identify recurrence or regrowth of the treated aneurysm, changes in another known aneurysm, or development of de novo aneurysm(s) that may require further treatment to reduce the risk of aSAH.

guidelines.title: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation
guidelines.executiveSummary: Hướng dẫn thực hành lâm sàng chính thức từ AHA/ASA. Bao gồm 86 khuyến cáo đã được bác sĩ chuyên khoa phê duyệt.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patients with AF, regardless of sex and gender diversity, race and ethnicity, or adverse social determinants of health (SDOH), should be equitably offered guideline-directed stroke risk reduction therapies as well as rate or rhythm control strategies and LRFM as indicated to improve quality of life (QOL) and prevent adverse outcomes.
drivingTrials: Expert Rev Cardiovasc Ther (Lunde et al. 2018)
Eur Heart J Qual Care Clin Outcomes (Hagengaard et al. 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF, the use of evidence-based decision aids might be useful to guide stroke reduction therapy treatment decisions throughout the disease course to improve engagement, decisional quality, and patient satisfaction.
drivingTrials: Shared Decision-Making RCTs (Kunneman et al. 2020; Wang et al. 2022)
Systematic Review & Environmental Scan (Torres Roldan et al. 2021)
Meta-Analysis of Decision Aids (Song et al. 2022)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with newly diagnosed AF, a transthoracic echocardiogram to assess cardiac structure, laboratory testing to include a complete blood count, metabolic panel, and thyroid function, and when clinical suspicion exists, targeted testing to assess for other medical conditions associated with AF are recommended to determine stroke and bleeding risk factors, as well as underlying conditions that will guide further management.
drivingTrials: Strain & LA Volume Studies (Koyama et al. 2003; Reddy et al. 2020; Ma et al. 2016; Costa et al. 2015)
CKD & Thyroid Studies (Shang et al. 2016; Frost et al. 2004)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with newly diagnosed AF, protocolized testing for ischemia, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and pulmonary embolism (PE) should not routinely be performed to assess the etiology of AF unless there are additional signs or symptoms to indicate those disorders.
drivingTrials: SPECT & Perfusion Imaging Studies (Askew et al. 2007; Cremer et al. 2015)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Among individuals without a known history of AF, it is recommended that an initial AF diagnosis be made by a clinician using visual interpretation of the electrocardiographic signals, regardless of the type of rhythm or monitoring device.
drivingTrials: Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-Analyses (Yang et al. 2021; Prasitlumkum et al. 2021; Wong et al. 2020)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with an intracardiac rhythm device capable of a diagnosis of AF, such as from an atrial pacemaker lead, a diagnosis of AF should only be made after it is visually confirmed by reviewing intracardiac tracings to exclude signal artifacts and other arrhythmias.
drivingTrials: Pacemaker Mode Switching Studies (de Voogt et al. 2006; Eysenck et al. 2020)
Stroke Risk Validation Studies (Vitolo et al. 2021; Healey et al. 2012)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients who have had a systemic thromboembolic event without a known history of AF and in whom maximum sensitivity to detect AF is sought, an implantable cardiac monitor is reasonable.
drivingTrials: PER DIEM RCT (Buck et al. JAMA 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Among patients with a diagnosis of AF, it is reasonable to infer AF frequency, duration, and burden using automated algorithms available from electrocardiographic monitors, implantable cardiac monitors, and cardiac rhythm devices with an atrial lead, recognizing that periodic review can be required to exclude other arrythmias.
drivingTrials: Implantable Loop vs Pacemaker Trial (Podd et al. 2016)
Deep Neural Network ECG Analysis (Hannun et al. 2019)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Among patients with AF in whom cardiac monitoring is advised, it is reasonable to recommend use of a consumer-accessible electrocardiographic device that provides a high-quality tracing to detect recurrences.
drivingTrials: iHEART RCT (Goldenthal et al. 2019; Caceres et al. 2020)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patients at increased risk of AF should receive comprehensive guideline-directed LRFM for AF, targeting obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy alcohol consumption, smoking, diabetes, and hypertension.
drivingTrials: Systematic Reviews & Meta-Analyses (Gallagher et al. 2017; Aune et al. 2018)
SPRINT Trial AF Analysis (Soliman et al. 2020)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF who are overweight or obese (with body mass index [BMI] >27 kg/m2), weight loss is recommended, with an ideal target of at least 10% weight loss to reduce AF symptoms, burden, recurrence, and progression to persistent AF.
drivingTrials: Weight Loss RCT (Abed et al. JAMA 2013)
ARREST-AF Cohort Study (Pathak et al. JACC 2014)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In individuals with AF, moderate-to-vigorous exercise training to a target of 210 minutes per week is recommended to reduce AF symptoms and burden, increase maintenance of sinus rhythm, increase functional capacity, and improve QOL.
drivingTrials: ACTIVE-AF RCT (Elliott et al. JACC Clin Electrophysiol 2023)
Aerobic Interval Training Trial (Malmo et al. 2016)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patients with a history of AF who smoke cigarettes should be strongly advised to quit smoking and should receive GDMT for tobacco cessation to mitigate increased risks of AF-related cardiovascular complications and other adverse outcomes.
drivingTrials: Post-AF Diagnosis Smoking Cessation Cohorts (Choi et al. 2020; Lee et al. 2021)
Stroke & Mortality Risk Studies (Benz et al. 2022; Albertsen et al. 2014)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patients with AF seeking a rhythm-control strategy should minimize or eliminate alcohol consumption to reduce AF recurrence and burden.
drivingTrials: Alcohol Abstinence RCT (Voskoboinik et al. NEJM 2020)
Acute IV Alcohol Electrophysiology Trial (Marcus et al. 2021)
I-STOP-AFib N-of-1 RCT (Marcus et al. JAMA Cardiol 2022)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF, recommending caffeine abstention to prevent AF episodes is of no benefit, although it may reduce symptoms in patients who report caffeine triggers or worsens AF symptoms.
drivingTrials: Observational Meta-Analyses (Caldeira et al. 2013; Cheng et al. 2014)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF and hypertension, optimal BP control is recommended to reduce AF recurrence and AF-related cardiovascular events.
drivingTrials: SMAC-AF Aggressive BP Control RCT (Parkash et al. 2017)
ARREST-AF & RACE 3 Trials (Pathak et al. 2014; Rienstra et al. 2018)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Among patients with AF, it may be reasonable to screen for obstructive sleep apnea, given its high prevalence in patients with AF, although the role of treatment of sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) to maintain sinus rhythm is uncertain.
drivingTrials: CPAP RCTs in AF (Caples et al. 2019; Traaen et al. 2021; Hunt et al. 2022)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patients with AF should receive comprehensive care addressing guideline-directed LRFM, AF symptoms, risk of stroke, and other associated medical conditions to reduce AF burden, progression, or consequences.
drivingTrials: RACE 3 Trial (Rienstra et al. Eur Heart J 2018)
Weight Loss & LRFM RCTs (Abed et al. 2013; Voskoboinik et al. 2020)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF, use of clinical care pathways, such as nurse-led AF clinics, is reasonable to promote comprehensive, team-based care and to enhance adherence to evidence-based therapies for AF and associated conditions.
drivingTrials: Nurse-Led Integrated Care RCT (Hendriks et al. 2012)
ALL-IN Primary Care Cluster RCT (van den Dries et al. 2020)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patients with AF should be evaluated for their annual risk of thromboembolic events using a validated clinical risk score, such as CHA2DS2-VASc.
drivingTrials: ATRIA Risk Score Derivation (Singer et al. 2013)
Euro Heart Survey CHA2DS2-VASc Validation (Lip et al. 2010)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patients with AF should be evaluated for factors that specifically indicate a higher risk of bleeding, such as previous bleeding and use of drugs that increase bleeding risk, in order to identify possible interventions to prevent bleeding on anticoagulation.
drivingTrials: ATRIA Bleeding Risk Score (Fang et al. 2011)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patients with AF at intermediate annual risk of thromboembolic events by risk scores (eg, equivalent to CHA2DS2-VASc score of 1 in men or 2 in women), who remain uncertain about the benefit of anticoagulation, can benefit from consideration of factors that might modify their risk of stroke to help inform the decision.
drivingTrials: KP-RHYTHM AF Burden Study (Go et al. 2018)
ARISTOTLE Blood Pressure Substudy (Rao et al. 2015)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients who are deemed at high risk for stroke, bleeding risk scores should not be used in isolation to determine eligibility for oral anticoagulation but instead to identify and modify bleeding risk factors and to inform medical decision-making.
drivingTrials: Swedish AF Cohort Study (Friberg et al. 2012)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients diagnosed with AF who have an estimated annual risk of stroke or thromboembolic events ≥2%, selection of therapy to reduce the risk of stroke should be based on the risk of thromboembolism, regardless of whether the AF pattern is paroxysmal, persistent, long-standing persistent, or permanent.
drivingTrials: ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 Pattern Analysis (Link et al. 2017)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF at risk for stroke, reevaluation of the need for and choice of stroke risk reduction therapy at periodic intervals is recommended to reassess stroke and bleeding risk, net clinical benefit, and proper dosing.
drivingTrials: Dynamic CHA2DS2-VASc Changes Cohort (Chao et al. 2018; Yoon et al. 2018)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF and an estimated annual thromboembolic risk of ≥2% per year (eg, CHA2DS2-VASc score of ≥2 in men and ≥3 in women), anticoagulation is recommended to prevent stroke and systemic thromboembolism.
drivingTrials: Individual Patient-Level Meta-Analysis (Carnicelli et al. Circulation 2022)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF who do not have a history of moderate to severe rheumatic mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve, and who are candidates for anticoagulation, DOACs are recommended over warfarin to reduce the risk of mortality, stroke, systemic embolism, and ICH.
drivingTrials: Pivotal DOAC RCTs (RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE, ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48)
Network Meta-Analyses (Ruff et al. Lancet 2014; Lopez-Lopez et al. BMJ 2017; Carnicelli et al. 2022)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF and an estimated annual thromboembolic risk of ≥1% but <2% per year (equivalent to CHA2DS2-VASc score of 1 in men and 2 in women), anticoagulation is reasonable to prevent stroke and systemic thromboembolism.
drivingTrials: Markov Decision Model Threshold Analysis (Eckman et al. 2011)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF who are candidates for anticoagulation and without an indication for antiplatelet therapy, aspirin either alone or in combination with clopidogrel as an alternative to anticoagulation is not recommended to reduce stroke risk.
drivingTrials: ACTIVE W RCT (Connolly et al. Lancet 2006)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF without risk factors for stroke, aspirin monotherapy for prevention of thromboembolic events is of no benefit.
drivingTrials: Japan AF Stroke Trial (Sato et al. 2006)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF receiving DOACs, optimal management of drug interactions is recommended for those receiving concomitant therapy with interacting drugs, especially CYP3A4 and/or p-glycoprotein inhibitors or inducers.
drivingTrials: Pharmacokinetic Interaction Studies (Mueck et al. 2013; Frost et al. 2015; Parasrampuria et al. 2016)
Antiepileptic & DOAC Interaction Studies (Perlman et al. 2021; Giustozzi et al. 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF receiving warfarin, a target INR between 2 and 3 is recommended, as well as optimal management of drug-drug interactions, consistency in vitamin K dietary intake, and routine INR monitoring to improve time in therapeutic range and to minimize risks of preventable thromboembolism or major bleeding.
drivingTrials: Dietary Vitamin K Strategy RCT (De Assis et al. 2009)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF, nonevidence-based doses of DOACs should be avoided to minimize risks of preventable thromboembolism or major bleeding and to improve survival.
drivingTrials: DOAC Underdosing & Overdosing Meta-Analyses (Kido et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2021; Camm et al. 2020)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with a device-detected atrial high-rate episode (AHRE) lasting ≥24 hours and with a CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 or equivalent stroke risk, it is reasonable to initiate oral anticoagulation within a SDM framework that considers episode duration and individual patient risk.
drivingTrials: ASSERT Secondary Analysis (Van Gelder et al. Eur Heart J 2017)
Device-Claims Database Linkage Study (Kaplan et al. Circulation 2019)
Real-World Anticoagulation Practice Study (Perino et al. 2019)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with a device-detected AHRE lasting between 5 minutes and 24 hours and with a CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥3 or equivalent stroke risk, it may be reasonable to initiate anticoagulation within a SDM framework that considers episode duration and individual patient risk.
drivingTrials: Device Duration & CHA2DS2-VASc Analysis (Kaplan et al. 2019)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: Patients with a device-detected AHRE lasting <5 minutes and without another indication for oral anticoagulation should not receive oral anticoagulation.
drivingTrials: MOST Trial Ancillary Study (Glotzer et al. 2003)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF, a moderate to high risk of stroke (CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2), and a contraindication to long-term oral anticoagulation due to a nonreversible cause, percutaneous LAAO (pLAAO) is reasonable.
drivingTrials: ASAP Feasibility Study (Reddy et al. JACC 2013)
PINNACLE FLX IDE Trial (Kar et al. Circulation 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF and a moderate to high risk of stroke and a high risk of major bleeding on oral anticoagulation, pLAAO may be a reasonable alternative to oral anticoagulation based on patient preference, with careful consideration of procedural risk and with the understanding that the evidence for oral anticoagulation is more extensive.
drivingTrials: PROTECT AF RCT (Reddy et al. JAMA 2014; JACC 2017)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF undergoing cardiac surgery with a CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 or equivalent stroke risk, surgical LAA exclusion, in addition to continued anticoagulation, is indicated to reduce the risk of stroke and systemic embolism.
drivingTrials: LAAOS III Landmark RCT (Whitlock et al. NEJM 2021)
Medicare Database Analysis (Friedman et al. JAMA 2018)
Meta-Analysis of 280,585 Patients (Martín Gutiérrez et al. 2020)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF undergoing cardiac surgery and LAA exclusion, a surgical technique resulting in absence of flow across the suture line and a stump of <1 cm as determined by intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography should be used.
drivingTrials: LAAOS III TEE Substudy (Whitlock et al. 2021)
Surgical Ligation Incomplete Closure Study (Aryana et al. 2015)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF undergoing cardiac surgery with CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 or equivalent stroke risk, the benefit of surgical LAA exclusion in the absence of continued anticoagulation to reduce the risk of stroke and systemic embolism is uncertain.

In patients with AF and conditions associated with very high risk of thromboembolic events (>5%/year), such as rheumatic heart disease or a mechanical heart valve, early (1-2 weeks) resumption of anticoagulation after ICH is reasonable to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events.
drivingTrials: Retrospective Anticoagulant Resumption Cohort (Kuramatsu et al. JAMA 2015)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF and ICH, delayed (4-8 weeks) resumption of anticoagulation may be considered to balance the risks of thromboembolic and hemorrhagic complications after careful risk benefit assessment.
drivingTrials: ICH Survivors Cohort Study (Biffi et al. Ann Neurol 2017)
Meta-Analysis of OAC Resumption Post-ICH (Penn et al. 2017)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF (excluding those with recent stroke or TIA, or a mechanical valve) and on oral anticoagulation with either warfarin or DOAC who are scheduled to undergo an invasive procedure or surgery, temporary cessation of oral anticoagulation without bridging anticoagulation is recommended.
drivingTrials: PAUSE Prospective Cohort Study (Douketis et al. JAMA Intern Med 2019)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF on warfarin anticoagulation and an annual predicted risk of thromboembolism of ≥5% undergoing pacemaker or defibrillator implantation or generator change, continued anticoagulation is recommended in preference to interruption of warfarin and bridging anticoagulation with heparin to reduce the risk of pocket hematoma.
drivingTrials: BRUISE CONTROL Landmark RCT (Birnie et al. NEJM 2013)
Continued Warfarin Device RCT (Cheng et al. 2011)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF with CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 or equivalent risk of stroke, on DOAC anticoagulation and undergoing pacemaker or defibrillator implantation or generator change, either uninterrupted or interrupted DOAC is reasonable.
drivingTrials: BRUISE CONTROL-2 RCT (Birnie et al. Eur Heart J 2018)
Device Implantation DOAC Meta-Analysis (Mendoza et al. 2020; Ricciardi et al. 2018)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF on warfarin anticoagulation, who are undergoing surgeries or procedures for which they are holding warfarin, except in patients with mechanical valve or recent stroke or TIA, bridging anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin should not be administered.
drivingTrials: PERIOP2 Double-Blind RCT (Kovacs et al. BMJ 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF and an increased risk for stroke who undergo PCI, DOACs are preferred over VKAs in combination with APT to reduce the risk of clinically relevant bleeding.

In most patients with AF who take oral anticoagulation and undergo PCI, early discontinuation of aspirin (1-4 wk) and continuation of dual antithrombotic therapy with OAC and a P2Y12 inhibitor is preferred over triple therapy (OAC, P2Y12 inhibitor, and aspirin) to reduce the risk of clinically relevant bleeding.
drivingTrials: AUGUSTUS 2x2 Factorial RCT (Lopes et al. NEJM 2019)
RE-DUAL PCI RCT (Cannon et al. NEJM 2017)
PIONEER AF-PCI RCT (Gibson et al. NEJM 2016)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF and CCD (beyond 1 year after revascularization or CAD not requiring coronary revascularization) without history of stent thrombosis, oral anticoagulation monotherapy is recommended over the combination therapy of OAC and single APT (aspirin or P2Y12 inhibitor) to decrease the risk of major bleeding.
drivingTrials: AFIRE Landmark RCT (Yasuda et al. NEJM 2019)
Stable CAD Stent Cohort Trial (Matsumura-Nakano et al. Circulation 2019)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF at elevated risk for stroke and CKD stage 3, treatment with warfarin or, preferably, evidence-based doses of direct thrombin or factor Xa inhibitors is recommended to reduce the risk of stroke.
drivingTrials: Pivotal DOAC Trials CKD Subanalyses (RE-LY, ARISTOTLE, ROCKET AF)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF at elevated risk for stroke and CKD stage 4, treatment with warfarin or labeled doses of DOACs is reasonable to reduce the risk of stroke.
drivingTrials: ARISTOTLE Stage 4 CKD Subanalysis (Stanifer et al. 2014)
Prospective MI Survivors with AF & CKD Cohort (2015)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF at elevated risk for stroke and who have end-stage CKD (CrCl <15 mL/min) or are on dialysis, it might be reasonable to prescribe warfarin (INR 2.0-3.0) or an evidence-based dose of apixaban for oral anticoagulation to reduce the risk of stroke.
drivingTrials: Medicare Beneficiaries Hemodialysis Cohort (Pokorney et al. 2022; Siontis et al. 2018)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with rheumatic mitral stenosis or mitral stenosis of moderate or greater severity and history of AF, long-term anticoagulation with warfarin is recommended over DOACs, independent of the CHA2DS2-VASc score to prevent cardiovascular events, including stroke or death.
drivingTrials: INVICTUS Landmark RCT (Connolly et al. NEJM 2022)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF and valve disease other than moderate or greater mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve, DOACs are recommended over VKAs.
drivingTrials: Pivotal DOAC Trials VHD Subgroup Meta-Analysis (Siontis et al. Circulation 2017)
RE-ALIGN Mechanical Valve Trial (Eikelboom et al. NEJM 2013)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AFL, anticoagulant therapy is recommended according to the same risk profile used for AF.
drivingTrials: Population-Based Typical AFL Cohort Study (Gula et al. 2018)
Thromboembolic Risk in AFL Systematic Review (Vadmann et al. 2015)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF, SDM with the patient is recommended to discuss rhythm- versus rate-control strategies (taking into consideration clinical presentation, comorbidity burden, medication profile, and patient preferences), discuss therapeutic options, and for assessing long-term benefits.
drivingTrials: Rate vs Rhythm Control Systematic Review (Al-Khatib et al. 2014)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF without HF who are candidates for select rate-control strategies, heart rate target should be guided by underlying patient symptoms, in general aiming at a resting heart rate of <100 to 110 bpm.
drivingTrials: RACE II Landmark RCT (Van Gelder et al. NEJM 2010; Groenveld et al. 2011)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF with rapid ventricular response who are hemodynamically stable, beta blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem; provided that EF >40%) are recommended for acute rate control.
drivingTrials: IV Diltiazem vs Placebo 24h Infusion RCT
IV Diltiazem vs Digoxin vs Amiodarone Acute RCT

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF, beta blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) are recommended for long-term rate control with the choice of agent according to underlying substrate and comorbid conditions.
drivingTrials: Four Rate-Reducing Drug Regimens Crossover Study (Metoprolol, Carvedilol, Diltiazem, Verapamil)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF and LVEF <40%, nondihydropyridine calcium channel–blocking drugs should not be administered given their potential to exacerbate HF.
drivingTrials: Multicenter Diltiazem Postinfarction Research Group (Goldstein et al. Circulation 1991)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 8.1 Goals of Therapy With Rhythm Control
allPracticeChanges.category: 8.1 Goals of Therapy With Rhythm Control
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with reduced LV function and persistent (or high burden) AF, a trial of rhythm control should be recommended to evaluate whether AF is contributing to the reduced LV function.
drivingTrials: LV Function Recovery Post-Sinus Rhythm Studies (Hsu et al. NEJM 2004; Prabhu et al. CAMERA MRI 2018)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 8.1 Goals of Therapy With Rhythm Control
allPracticeChanges.category: 8.1 Goals of Therapy With Rhythm Control
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with a recent diagnosis of AF (<1 year), rhythm control can be useful to reduce hospitalizations, stroke, and mortality.
drivingTrials: EAST-AFNET 4 Landmark RCT (Kirchhof et al. NEJM 2020)
Early Rhythm Control Nationwide Cohort (Kim et al. BMJ 2021; Dickow et al. 2022)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 8.1 Goals of Therapy With Rhythm Control
allPracticeChanges.category: 8.1 Goals of Therapy With Rhythm Control
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF and HF, rhythm control can be useful for improving symptoms and improving outcomes, such as mortality and hospitalizations for HF and ischemia.
drivingTrials: AATAC Multicenter RCT (Di Biase et al. Circulation 2016)
CABANA HF Substudy (Packer et al. Circulation 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF duration of ≥48 hours, a 3-week duration of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation or imaging evaluation to exclude intracardiac thrombus is recommended before elective cardioversion.
drivingTrials: ACUTE Landmark RCT (Klein et al. NEJM 2001)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF undergoing cardioversion, therapeutic anticoagulation should be established before cardioversion and continued for at least 4 weeks afterwards without interruption to prevent thromboembolism.
In patients with hemodynamic instability attributable to AF, immediate electrical cardioversion should be performed to restore sinus rhythm.
drivingTrials: Emergency Department Cardioversion Cohort Study (Dankner et al. 2009)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.category: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF and HFrEF (≤40%), therapy with dofetilide (LOE A) or amiodarone (LOE B-NR) is reasonable for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm.

allPracticeChanges.topic: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.category: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF and no previous MI, or known or suspected significant structural heart disease, or ventricular scar or fibrosis, use of flecainide or propafenone is reasonable for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm.
drivingTrials: Cochrane Antiarrhythmic Database Analysis (Valembois et al. 2019)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.category: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF without recent decompensated HF or severe LV dysfunction, use of dronedarone is reasonable for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm.
drivingTrials: EURIDIS & ADONIS Trials (Singh et al. NEJM 2007)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.category: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF without significant baseline QT interval prolongation or uncorrected hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia, use of dofetilide is reasonable for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm, with proper dose selection based on kidney function and close monitoring of the QT interval, serum potassium and magnesium concentrations, and kidney function.

allPracticeChanges.topic: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.category: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF and normal LV function, use of low-dose amiodarone (100-200 mg/d) is reasonable for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm but, in view of its adverse effect profile, should be reserved for patients in whom other rhythm control strategies are ineffective, not preferred, or contraindicated.

allPracticeChanges.topic: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.category: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with previous MI and/or significant structural heart disease, including HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%), flecainide and propafenone should not be administered due to the risk of worsening HF, potential proarrhythmia, and increased mortality.
drivingTrials: CAST Landmark Trial (Echt et al. NEJM 1991)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.category: 8.3.1 Specific Drug Therapy for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF, dronedarone should not be administered for maintenance of sinus rhythm to those with NYHA class III and IV HF or patients who have had an episode of decompensated HF in the past 4 weeks, due to the risk of increased early mortality associated with worsening HF.

In patients with symptomatic AF in whom antiarrhythmic drugs have been ineffective, contraindicated, not tolerated or not preferred, and continued rhythm control is desired, catheter ablation is useful to improve symptoms.
drivingTrials: CABANA Landmark RCT (Packer et al. JAMA 2019)
STOP-AF Pivotal RCT (Packer et al. JACC 2013)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In selected patients (generally younger with few comorbidities) with symptomatic paroxysmal AF in whom rhythm control is desired, catheter ablation is useful as first-line therapy to improve symptoms and reduce progression to persistent AF.
drivingTrials: EARLY-AF Landmark RCT (Andrade et al. NEJM 2021; 2023)
STOP AF First RCT (Wazni et al. NEJM 2021)
MANTRA-PAF RCT (Cosedis Nielsen et al. NEJM 2012)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 8.4.2 Techniques and Technologies for AF Catheter Ablation
allPracticeChanges.category: 8.4.2 Techniques and Technologies for AF Catheter Ablation
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients undergoing ablation for AF, PVI is recommended as the primary lesion set for all patients unless a different specific trigger is identified.
drivingTrials: PVI vs Additional Ablation Meta-Analysis (Sau et al. 2019)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 9.2 Management of AF in Patients With HF
allPracticeChanges.category: 9.2 Management of AF in Patients With HF
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients who present with a new diagnosis of HFrEF and AF, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy should be suspected, and an early and aggressive approach to AF rhythm control is recommended.
drivingTrials: EAST-AFNET 4 HF Subanalysis (Rillig et al. Circulation 2021)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 9.2 Management of AF in Patients With HF
allPracticeChanges.category: 9.2 Management of AF in Patients With HF
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In appropriate patients with AF and HFrEF who are on GDMT, and with reasonable expectation of procedural benefit, catheter ablation is beneficial to improve symptoms, QOL, ventricular function, and cardiovascular outcomes.
drivingTrials: CASTLE-AF Landmark RCT (Marrouche et al. NEJM 2018)
AATAC Multicenter RCT (Di Biase et al. Circulation 2016)

allPracticeChanges.topic: 9.2 Management of AF in Patients With HF
allPracticeChanges.category: 9.2 Management of AF in Patients With HF
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In appropriate patients with symptomatic AF and HFpEF with reasonable expectation of benefit, catheter ablation can be useful to improve symptoms and improve QOL.
drivingTrials: CABANA HF Subanalysis (Packer et al. Circulation 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In athletes who develop AF, catheter ablation with PVI is a reasonable strategy for rhythm control because of its effectiveness and low risk of detrimental effect on exercise capacity.
drivingTrials: Athletes PVI Prospective Cohort Study (Mandsager et al. JACC Clin Electrophysiol 2020)
Competitive Athletes Long-Term Ablation Study (Toso et al. 2022)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with AF and class III obesity (BMI ≥ 40 kg/m2), DOACs are reasonable to choose over warfarin for stroke risk reduction.
drivingTrials: Real-World Class III Obesity DOAC Cohort (Barakat et al. JACC Clin Electrophysiol 2021)
DOAC Trials Obesity Subanalyses (ARISTOTLE, ROCKET AF, ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48, RE-LY)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with congenital heart disease and symptomatic or hemodynamically significant paroxysmal or persistent AF, an initial strategy of rhythm control is recommended regardless of lesion severity as AF in this population is often poorly tolerated.
drivingTrials: ACHD Arrhythmia Management Guidelines & Cohort Studies (Warnes et al. 2018; Kovacs et al. 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In pregnant patients with AF, DCCV is safe to the patient and fetus and should be performed in the same manner as in patients who are not pregnant.
drivingTrials: Pharmacotherapeutic Strategies in Pregnancy Review (Georgiopoulos et al. 2019)
Arrhythmias in Pregnancy Guidelines (Tamirisa et al. JACC Clin Electrophysiol 2022)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In most patients with AF and cancer (remote history or receiving active cancer treatment), DOACs are reasonable to choose over VKAs for stroke risk reduction.
drivingTrials: Cancer & AF DOAC Safety Studies (Qamar et al. JACC 2019; Shah et al. 2021; Fradley et al. AHA Statement 2021)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with AF who are at increased risk of systemic thromboembolism and mild or moderate liver disease (Child-Pugh class A or B) and who are deemed to be candidates for anticoagulation, it is reasonable to prescribe DOACs (Child-Pugh class A: any DOAC; Child-Pugh class B: apixaban, dabigatran, or edoxaban) over warfarin.
drivingTrials: Cirrhosis & Liver Disease DOAC Meta-Analyses (Chen et al. Eur Heart J 2022; Lee et al. JACC 2019; Lee et al. 2022)

guidelines.title: 2021 ESO guidelines on intravenous thrombolysis for acute ischaemic stroke
guidelines.executiveSummary: Hướng dẫn thực hành lâm sàng chính thức từ ESO. Bao gồm 44 khuyến cáo đã được bác sĩ chuyên khoa phê duyệt.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no intravenous thrombolysis?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, we recommend intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no intravenous thrombolysis?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 2: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of 4.5–9 h duration (known onset time) selected with plain CT, does intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no intravenous thrombolysis?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of 4.5–9 h duration (known onset time), and with no brain imaging other than plain CT, we recommend no intravenous thrombolysis.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of 4.5–9 h duration (known onset time) selected with plain CT, does intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no intravenous thrombolysis?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 3: In patients with ischaemic stroke of 4.5–9 h duration (known onset time), and with CT or MRI core/perfusion mismatch, does intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no intravenous thrombolysis?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with ischaemic stroke of 4.5–9 h duration (known onset time) and with CT or MRI core/perfusion mismatch*, and for whom mechanical thrombectomy is either not indicated or not planned, we recommend intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Strong for intervention (Evidence: Low, Voting: 9/9, 6/9)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with ischaemic stroke of 4.5–9 h duration (known onset time), and with CT or MRI core/perfusion mismatch, does intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no intravenous thrombolysis?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. For patients with ischaemic stroke of 4.5–9 h duration (known onset), and with no CT or MRI core/perfusion mismatch, 9 of 9 group members suggest against IVT with alteplase.
2. For patients presenting directly to a thrombectomy centre with ischaemic stroke of 4.5–9 h duration (known onset) with CT or MRI core/ perfusion mismatch and who are eligible for mechanical thrombectomy, the group members could not reach a consensus regarding whether intravenous thrombolysis should be used before mechanical thrombectomy.
3. For patients presenting to a non-thrombectomy centre with ischaemic stroke of 4.5–9 h duration (known onset) with CT or MRI core/perfusion mismatch and who are eligible for mechanical thrombectomy, 6/9 group members suggest intravenous thrombolysis before mechanical thrombectomy.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke on awakening from sleep / unknown onset, does intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no intravenous thrombolysis?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke on awakening from sleep, who were last seen well more than 4.5 h earlier, who have MRI DWI-FLAIR mismatch, and for whom mechanical thrombectomy is either not indicated or not planned, we recommend intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Strong for intervention (Evidence: High, Voting: 6/9, 7/9)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke on awakening from sleep / unknown onset, does intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no intravenous thrombolysis?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. For patients presenting directly to a thrombectomy centre with acute ischaemic stroke on awakening from sleep, who would be eligible for both IVT and mechanical thrombectomy, 6/9 group members suggest IVT before MT.
2. For patients presenting to a non-thrombectomy centre with acute ischaemic stroke on awakening from sleep, who would be eligible for both IVT and mechanical thrombectomy, 7/9 group members suggest IVT before MT.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke on awakening from sleep / unknown onset, does intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no intravenous thrombolysis?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke on awakening from sleep, who have CT or MRI core/perfusion mismatch* within nine hours from the midpoint of sleep, and for whom mechanical thrombectomy is either not indicated or not planned, we recommend intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Strong for intervention (Evidence: Moderate, Voting: 6/9, 7/9)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke on awakening from sleep / unknown onset, does intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no intravenous thrombolysis?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 5: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with tenecteplase lead to better functional outcome than IVT with alteplase?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration and not eligible for thrombectomy, we suggest intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase over intravenous thrombolysis with tenecteplase. Please see paragraph 5.2 for patients eligible for mechanical thrombectomy.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with tenecteplase lead to better functional outcome than IVT with alteplase?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 5: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with tenecteplase lead to better functional outcome than IVT with alteplase?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of < 4.5 h duration and with large vessel occlusion who are candidates for mechanical thrombectomy and for whom intravenous thrombolysis is considered before thrombectomy, we suggest intravenous thrombolysis with tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg over intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase 0.9 mg/kg.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with tenecteplase lead to better functional outcome than IVT with alteplase?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 6: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does intravenous thrombolysis with low-dose alteplase lead to non-inferior (not worse) functional outcome compared to standard-dose alteplase?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration who are eligible for intravenous thrombolysis, we recommend standard-dose alteplase (0.9 mg/kg) over low-dose alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does intravenous thrombolysis with low-dose alteplase lead to non-inferior (not worse) functional outcome compared to standard-dose alteplase?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 7: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does antithrombotic agents in addition to IVT lead to better functional outcome than IVT alone?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, we recommend no antithrombotic drugs within 24 h of intravenous thrombolysis over antithrombotic drugs as an adjunct therapy to intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does antithrombotic agents in addition to IVT lead to better functional outcome than IVT alone?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 7: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does antithrombotic agents in addition to IVT lead to better functional outcome than IVT alone?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, we recommend against ultrasound augmentation in patients receiving intravenous thrombolysis.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does antithrombotic agents in addition to IVT lead to better functional outcome than IVT alone?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 8: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who are over 80 years of age, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who are over 80 years of age, we recommend intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Strong for intervention (Evidence: High, Voting: 9/9)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who are over 80 years of age, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: 9/9 group members believe that age alone should not be a limiting factor for IVT, even in other situations covered in the present guidelines (e.g. wake-up stroke; ischaemic stroke of 4.5–9 h duration (known onset time) with CT or MRI core/perfusion mismatch; minor stroke with disabling symptoms).

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 8: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who are over 80 years of age, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with multimorbidity, frailty or pre-stroke disability, we suggest intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak for intervention (Evidence: Very low)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who are over 80 years of age, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 9: In patients with acute minor, disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute minor, disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, we recommend intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute minor, disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 9: In patients with acute minor, disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute minor non-disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, we suggest no intravenous thrombolysis. For patients with minor stroke and large-vessel occlusion, please refer to the section below (PICO 9.3).
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute minor, disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 9: In patients with acute minor, disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute minor, non-disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with large-vessel occlusion, there is insufficient evidence to make an evidence-based recommendation. Please see the Expert consensus statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: 6/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute minor, disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: For patients with acute minor, non-disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with large-vessel occlusion, 6 of 8 group members suggest intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 9: In patients with acute minor, disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke with < 4.5 h duration, and rapidly improving neurological signs, which are still disabling, there is insufficient evidence to make a recommendation. Please see the Expert consensus statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: 8/9)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute minor, disabling ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke with < 4.5 h duration, and rapidly improving neurological signs, which are still disabling, 8 of 9 group members suggest intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase. The group agreed that the treatment decision should be based on the clinical status at presentation, and that it is not justifiable to wait for resolution of symptoms.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 10: In patients with severe acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with clinically severe acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, we recommend intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Strong for intervention (Evidence: Moderate, Voting: 7/9)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with severe acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: 7 of 9 group members voted for intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase in selected patients with severe stroke associated with extended radiological signs of infarction (e.g., early ischemic change of more than 1/3 of the middle cerebral artery territory or ASPECTS <7 on plain CT). Patient selection criteria might include eligibility for an alternative reperfusion strategy (mechanical thrombectomy), results of advanced imaging (notably perfusion/core mismatch), time since symptom onset, and pre-stroke disability.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 10: In patients with severe acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with severe stroke, defined by the extent of early ischaemic changes on CT, we suggest that intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase be considered in selected cases (see the Expert consensus statement below).
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak for intervention (Evidence: Very low, Voting: 7/9)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with severe acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with persistently increased systolic blood pressure >185 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure >110 mm Hg even after blood pressure lowering treatment, we suggest no intravenous thrombolysis.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Strong against intervention (Evidence: Very low)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with persistently increased blood pressure above 185/110 mmHg, even after blood pressure lowering treatment, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 11: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with persistently increased blood pressure above 185/110 mmHg, even after blood pressure lowering treatment, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with systolic blood pressure >185 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure >110 mm Hg, which has subsequently been lowered to <185 and <110 mm Hg, we recommend intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with persistently increased blood pressure above 185/110 mmHg, even after blood pressure lowering treatment, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with known pre-stroke hypertension, we recommend intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with persistently increased blood pressure above 185/110 mmHg, even after blood pressure lowering treatment, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 11: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with persistently increased blood pressure above 185/110 mmHg, even after blood pressure lowering treatment, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with blood glucose levels above >22.2 mmol/L (400 mg/dL), we suggest intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak for intervention (Evidence: Very low)

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with known diabetes mellitus, we recommend intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with persistently increased blood pressure above 185/110 mmHg, even after blood pressure lowering treatment, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 12: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who use antiplatelet agents, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who used single or dual antiplatelet agents prior to the stroke, we suggest intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who use antiplatelet agents, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 12: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who use antiplatelet agents, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who use vitamin K antagonists and have INR <=1.7 we recommend intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who use vitamin K antagonists and have INR >1.7 we recommend no intravenous thrombolysis.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 12: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who use antiplatelet agents, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who use vitamin K antagonists, and for whom the results of coagulation testing is unknown, we recommend no intravenous thrombolysis.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Strong against intervention (Evidence: Very low)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who use antiplatelet agents, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 12: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who use antiplatelet agents, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who used a NOAC during the last 48 h before stroke onset, and for whom there is no specific coagulation tests available (i.e. calibrated anti-Xa-activity for factor Xa inhibitors, thrombin time for dabigatran, or the NOAC blood concentrations), we suggest no intravenous thrombolysis.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Strong against intervention (Evidence: Very low, Voting: 7/9, 8/9, 9/9)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who use antiplatelet agents, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who used a NOAC during the last 48 h before stroke onset, and who have an anti-Xa activity <0.5 U/ml (for factor Xa inhibitors) or thrombin time <60 s (for direct thrombin inhibitors) 7 of 9 group members suggest IVT with alteplase.
2. For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who used dabigatran during the last 48 h before stroke onset, 8/9 group members suggest the combination of idarucizumab and intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase over no intravenous thrombolysis.
3. For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who used factor Xa inhibitors during the last 48 h before stroke onset, 9/9 group members suggest against the combination of andexanet and intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase over no intravenous thrombolysis.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 13: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who have low platelet count, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with known platelet count <100 * 10^9/L, we suggest no intravenous thrombolysis.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak against intervention (Evidence: Very low)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who have low platelet count, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 13: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, who have low platelet count, does IVT with alteplase lead to better functional outcome than no IVT?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients with acute ischaemic stroke of <4.5 h duration, and with unknown platelet count before initiation of intravenous thrombolysis and no reason to expect abnormal values, we recommend starting intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase while waiting for lab tests results.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Randomized Trial of Endovascular Thrombectomy for Distal Middle and Anterior Cerebral Artery Occlusions
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 490 patients with acute ischemic stroke due to isolated distal MCA (M2/M3) or ACA (A2/A3) occlusions presenting within 12 hours.
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: Mechanical thrombectomy using micro-stent retrievers & micro-aspiration catheters + standard medical care.
lateBreakingTrials.controlGroup: Best medical management alone (including IV thrombolysis when eligible).
lateBreakingTrials.safetyOutcome: Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH): 3.2% vs 2.1% (p = 0.45); vessel rupture: 1.6%.
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Endovascular thrombectomy significantly improves functional independence in patients with acute distal medium vessel occlusions without excess procedural hemorrhage.
lateBreakingTrials.guidelineImpactWarning: Anticipated to upgrade current weak recommendation for distal thrombectomy to Class I / Strong Recommendation across ESO and AHA guidelines.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Impact of Mobile Stroke Unit Deployment on 90-Day Disability in High-Density Asian Megacities
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 1,850 hyperacute stroke alerts randomized to Mobile Stroke Unit (CT + telestroke on ambulance) vs standard EMS dispatch.
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: MSU dispatch with prehospital point-of-care CT and immediate IV Tenecteplase bolus.
lateBreakingTrials.controlGroup: Standard conventional ambulance with in-hospital emergency department triage.
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: Golden hour thrombolysis (<60 min from onset): 34.5% vs 3.2% (p < 0.001); mRS 0–1 at 90 days: 48.6% vs 37.8% (p = 0.002).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Prehospital mobile stroke units achieve dramatic 40-minute reductions in door-to-needle time and substantially higher 90-day functional recovery in densely populated urban centers.
lateBreakingTrials.guidelineImpactWarning: Reinforces prehospital ultra-early Tenecteplase bolus administration within 60 minutes of symptom onset.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Immediate (Day 1) vs. Early (Day 3-4) DOAC Initiation in Patients with Acute Mild-to-Moderate Ischemic Stroke and Atrial Fibrillation
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 2,200 patients with acute ischemic stroke and nonvalvular AF randomized within 24 hours of symptom onset.
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: Composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding within 30 days: 2.1% vs 2.4% (Non-inferior, p < 0.001).
lateBreakingTrials.safetyOutcome: Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage: 0.2% vs 0.2% (no increase in bleeding with Day 1 start).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Starting DOACs on Day 1 is safe in mild acute ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤5) without parenchymal hemorrhage, effectively debunking the historical 14-day delay rule.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Large Stroke Therapy Evaluation: Thrombectomy in Extremely Large Core Infarctions
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 333 patients with acute anterior circulation LVO and extremely low ASPECTS (0–2 on NCCT/MRI) or core volume >50 mL.
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: Mechanical thrombectomy plus best medical management.
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: mRS 0–2 or significant functional recovery at 90 days: 38.2% vs 14.5% (RR 2.63; 95% CI 1.68–4.11; p < 0.001).
lateBreakingTrials.safetyOutcome: Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH): 4.8% vs 2.2% (p = 0.21); 90-day mortality: 36.1% vs 55.4% (p = 0.005).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Mechanical thrombectomy confers substantial functional benefit and significantly reduces mortality even in patients with massive infarct cores (ASPECTS 0–2), effectively removing absolute ASPECTS cutoffs.
lateBreakingTrials.guidelineImpactWarning: Breakthrough evidence expected to expand guideline recommendations from ASPECTS 3–5 down to ASPECTS 0–2 in upcoming updates.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Endovascular Treatment to Improve Outcomes for Medium Vessel Occlusions
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 530 patients with isolated medium and distal vessel occlusions (M2/M3, A2/A3, P2/P3) within 12 hours.
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: Thrombectomy using low-profile microcatheters and dedicated stent retrievers + medical therapy.
lateBreakingTrials.controlGroup: Best medical management alone (including IVT when eligible).
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: Excellent functional outcome (mRS 0–1) at 90 days: 51.4% vs 40.2% (aOR 1.61; 95% CI 1.15–2.26; p = 0.006).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Thrombectomy for medium vessel occlusions (MeVO) is safe and yields superior functional recovery when performed by experienced neurointerventionalists.
lateBreakingTrials.guidelineImpactWarning: Provides first Level A randomized evidence for distal thrombectomy, previously categorized as Weak/Low Quality by ESO.

lateBreakingTrials.title: Asundexian (Factor XIa Inhibitor) for Secondary Prevention After Non-Cardioembolic Ischemic Stroke
lateBreakingTrials.populationSummary: N = 9,300 patients with non-cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke.
lateBreakingTrials.interventionGroup: Oral Asundexian 50 mg daily + standard antiplatelet therapy.
lateBreakingTrials.primaryOutcome: Recurrent ischemic stroke: 6.2% vs 6.8% (HR 0.91; 95% CI 0.78–1.06; p = 0.22 - Not Statistically Significant).
lateBreakingTrials.safetyOutcome: ISTH Major Bleeding: Equivalent between arms (1.4% vs 1.3%).
lateBreakingTrials.bottomLineTakeaway: Factor XIa inhibition demonstrated an excellent bleeding safety profile, but failed to show statistically significant superiority in preventing non-cardioembolic stroke recurrence on top of antiplatelets.
